title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
trick: Re-run every simulator input an agent wrote and search every tool result it received, so each wrong answer is labeled computed-wrong, never-seen, or seen-and-misread; retrieval's cost sits in the last two.
framing_stripped: Called 'evidence substitution' and a 'build / exposure / closure' localization of where retrieval costs accuracy; it is a three-factor product decomposition of multiple-choice accuracy (did the agent's own PHREEQC run print the keyed number, did that number reach the agent's context, did the agent then pick the matching option) made exact by re-executing a deterministic simulator offline, applied to one harness knob (paste the report into context vs hand the agent a section index and let it read line ranges), followed by a three-sentence prompt fix that tells the agent which file is authoritative.
method_equations: Per numeric item, accuracy decomposes exactly as $A = p\,s\,c + u$, where $p$ = build rate (share of trajectories whose own simulation printed the keyed value), $s$ = exposure rate (share of built trajectories in which the keyed value appeared in some tool result the agent received: inline payload, read_file result or search match), $c$ = closure rate (share of exposed trajectories that answered correctly), and $u$ = accuracy contributed by answers given without the keyed value in view (nearest-option picks and guesses) (sec. 2.3). The change between a retrieval condition and the same model's logged inline run, $\Delta A = A^{\mathrm{TOC}} - A^{\mathrm{inline}}$, is attributed to the four factors $k \in \{p, s, c, u\}$ by Shapley values: $\phi_k = \sum_{S \subseteq F \setminus \{k\}} \frac{|S|!\,(|F|-|S|-1)!}{|F|!}\,[A(S \cup \{k\}) - A(S)]$, where $F$ is the set of four factors, $A(S)$ is the accuracy formula evaluated with the factors in $S$ at their TOC values and the rest at their inline values, and $\sum_k \phi_k = \Delta A$; 95% intervals come from 1,000 item bootstraps resampling items jointly for both conditions (sec. 2.3, Table 9). A keyed value counts as present when a printed number equals the option at its printed precision or rounds to it when printed with more digits; midpoints match both neighbors (App. C). The truncation trap rate is $\tau = n_{\mathrm{chose\ distractor}} / n_{\mathrm{trap}}$, where $n_{\mathrm{trap}}$ = trajectories that saw a value which rounds to the key but truncates to a neighboring option, each trajectory counted once (Table 4). The paired replay freezes GPT-5.2's inline run at its first exit-code-zero execution at turn $s$ on 131 numeric items and continues the identical history twice with budget $24 - s$ turns, once with the report inline and once with the index; the estimate is $\bar{\Delta} = \frac{1}{131}\sum_{i} \frac{1}{3}\sum_{r=1}^{3} [y^{\mathrm{TOC}}_{i,r} - y^{\mathrm{inline}}_{i,r}]$ with $y \in \{0,1\}$ the correctness of repeat $r$ on item $i$, interval from 50,000 paired-item bootstrap resamples (App. D, Table 10).
load_bearing_assumption: That the two interfaces are information-equivalent so that any gap is a usable-information loss, not a content loss: every number in the inline report is one read_file call away under TOC, and the paired replay fixes files by hash (sec. 6, App. D). Two things carry this: (1) re-executing the agent's input with PHREEQC 3.8.6 reproduces what the agent actually saw (4,971 of 5,009 last executions reproduce the stored report exactly, the rest differ in line order; sec. 2.3), and (2) 'seen' means a numeric match at option precision anywhere in a tool result the agent received, which the manual audit confirms on 52 of 58 numeric trajectories, with five of six disagreements being a matching number printed for a different reaction step (App. C). If either fails, the exposure/closure split is noise.
weakest_component: The distractor design makes the headline mechanism possible: for numeric items 'distractors typically differ from the key in the last printed digit' (sec. 2.1), so a truncation error (2.75065 written as 2.750 for key 2.751) lands exactly on a wrong option. A critic says evidence substitution costs accuracy only on a benchmark built so that misrounding equals a distractor; on 137 numeric items the trap cases are 35 (GPT-5.2) and 27 (GPT-5.1) trajectories, and they explain 'about two thirds' of seen-but-wrong TOC trajectories (sec. 4). Second target: the condition confound the authors concede in App. B: the system-prompt line describing execute_phreeqc differs by condition (inline 'use read_file only if you need'; TOC 'use read_file to inspect results'), so reading behaviour is partly induced by the description; the only clean comparison is the paired replay, done for one model (GPT-5.2) on 131 items, three repeats. Third: the decomposition's reference is a single logged inline run per model, and run-to-run variance is of the effect's size: GPT-5.2 TOC vs inline is $-11.4$ pp on the three reruns but $-5.1$ pp [$-16.1$, $+5.8$] on the TOC control run (Table 9), and the pooled GPT-5.2 contrast is not significant after Holm correction ($p = 0.128$; Table 1). Fourth: decoding is not matched across vendors (Claude at temperature 0 without extended thinking, GPT at API defaults), and the paper does not identify the model property behind the GPT/Claude split (sec. 9). Fifth: in the outcome-selected manual audit of 24 TOC losses only 7 were caused by the retrieval channel and 15 were build failures that churn between runs (App. C), so the mechanism is a minority of item-level losses and is visible only through the aggregate decomposition.
regime: One deterministic scientific tool, PHREEQC 3.8.6 (USGS aqueous geochemistry), reports up to 846.8k characters; 158 four-option multiple-choice items (137 numeric) from 19 setups, re-verified by execution from a 200-item pool (42 items defective: 17 unstable redox values, 9 missing units, 1 wrong key; App. A). Six closed API models: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6 (temperature 0, no extended thinking), GPT-5.4, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Flash Preview (API defaults). Agent: four tools (write_file, read_file with line ranges, list_file, execute_phreeqc), one tool call per turn, at most 24 steps, answer committed to a file. Conditions: Raw100k (report inlined, head/tail-truncated at 100,000 characters), TOC (section index, at most 50 entries), Grep (metadata plus regex search), Hybrid (inline when it fits, else TOC), TOC+Report and TOC+Round (three-sentence instructions). 5,773 logged trajectories, 11,007 re-executed simulator calls; mean input tokens per item 28.3k to 100.1k. Headline accuracies (Table 1): Direct 25.9-43.0%; agents inline 65.8-91.1% (Claude/GPT), TOC 57.0-91.8%; TOC minus inline pooled: Opus $-0.6$, Sonnet $-0.5$, GPT-5.4 $+0.2$, GPT-5.2 $-7.9$ [$-14.9$, $-0.9$], GPT-5.1 $-11.3$ [$-18.0$, $-4.9$] pp. Stage rates under TOC (Table 3): GPT-5.2 $p = 62.5$, $s = 90.7$, $c = 82.4$%; Sonnet $p = 86.9$, $s = 98.9$, $c = 98.0$%. Report skipped in 60.3% (GPT-5.2), 53.0% (GPT-5.1), 41.8% (GPT-5.4), 10.5% (Sonnet) of TOC trajectories; trap rate 26/35, 19/27, 15/31, 1/35 (Table 4). Interventions over all TOC runs: TOC+Report $+7.9$ (GPT-5.2), $+6.3$ (GPT-5.1), $+7.8$ pp (GPT-5.4); TOC+Round $+0.6$ / $+1.2$ pp; Hybrid $+4.6$ / $+8.0$ pp over the TOC control (Table 5). Paired replay, GPT-5.2: $-9.4$ pp [$-14.5$, $-4.6$] (Table 10). Gemini 3 Flash excluded: no parseable answer on 46% of items inline, 71% under TOC (App. E).
information_asymmetry: Four asymmetries. (1) Hindsight re-execution vs the run. The paper knows, after the fact, the full produced corpus (every output of every re-executed input) and the full seen corpus (every tool result the agent received) and so labels each trajectory build / exposure / closure without a judge (sec. 2.3, App. C). The agent at answer time has only the seen corpus, and the harness at run time has the produced corpus but does not use it: the check 'does the number the agent is about to submit appear in result.out at the options' precision' needs no answer key and is never built; the paper's remedy is a static prompt line instead (Table 5, App. B). (2) Harness-design time vs inference. Which file is authoritative and at what precision each file prints is known when the harness is written (result.out prints at the options' precision; SELECTED_OUTPUT prints more digits) and is absent from the agent's view under TOC, where the report competes with the agent's own files; moving that one fact into the tool description and every tool result cuts report skipping from 57.0% to 0.0% (GPT-5.2) and lifts closure from 83.5% to 98.8%, while telling the agent how to round (TOC+Round, same budget of three sentences, no file named) leaves closure at 81.5% and the trap rate at 17/25 (sec. 5, Table 5). The agent has the rounding rule and the options' precision in context and still truncates; the missing information is not the rule but the pointer. (3) Leaderboard vs stage. Net accuracy change hides offsetting stage moves: GPT-5.4 gains $+4.1$ pp [$+0.0$, $+8.1$] in build under TOC and loses $-2.6$ (exposure) and $-7.2$ pp [$-11.1$, $-4.2$] (closure), net $-4.4$ pp [$-12.4$, $+3.4$] and pooled $+0.2$ pp (sec. 4); a harness choosing delivery by final accuracy sees nothing to fix. The stage-level signal exists in the logs of every run and is computed by no leaderboard. (4) For L4 specifically: this is a lossy-context measurement with the content held fixed, and it was possible only because the tool is deterministic and the needed fact is a scalar that can be matched numerically, so 'was the fact present in what the agent read' has a ground-truth answer. For compaction summaries, memory files and sub-agent return briefs the same question (was the needed fact present, was it used) has no such oracle; the paper's design says what such an oracle must deliver (a produced corpus, a seen corpus, a matcher, a fixed-computation paired replay) and does not say how to get one for non-deterministic tool output. The paper also leaves open what model property drives the split (sec. 9), whether reasoning effort removes it (all GPT runs at API default effort), and whether the agents read their own files 'simply because they are short' (sec. 4), so the causal account of substitution is one intervention deep.
occupies: The build / exposure / closure decomposition of tool-using agent accuracy by offline re-execution of a deterministic simulator, its Shapley attribution across delivery conditions, the result that GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 pp when a PHREEQC report is delivered by section index instead of inline while Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 show no net cost (GPT-5.4's being an offsetting build gain and closure loss), the named failure 'evidence substitution' (answering from one's own higher-precision output file and truncating to a neighboring option), the fixed-computation paired replay showing $-9.4$ pp for GPT-5.2, and the finding that naming the authoritative output file (+6.3 to +7.9 pp) or inlining what fits fixes it while a rounding instruction does not.

neighbors.title: Is Grep All You Need? How Agent Harnesses Reshape Agentic Search
neighbors.trick: Compare grep against vector retrieval on 116 LongMemEval questions across a custom harness and three provider CLIs, with tool results either inline or written to files the model reads separately; grep usually wins and the harness and tool-result style move accuracy as much as the retriever does, with no account of why.

neighbors.title: PHREEQC-MCQ-200: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Tool-Augmented Scientific Simulator Agents
neighbors.trick: 200 multiple-choice geochemistry items that require writing and running PHREEQC inputs; reports that tool access raises aggregate accuracy but loses items answered correctly without tools, and that a table-of-contents output interface saves tokens for strong models and hurts mid-tier ones; this card's paper re-verifies its keys (42 of 200 defective) and locates the interface cost.

neighbors.title: Bayes-Sufficient Compression Is Not Enough: How Does Communication Help Multi-Agent Systems?
neighbors.trick: Model a sender-executor pair where message value is receiver gain minus protocol tax, show that a message preserving all decision-relevant content still fails a bounded receiver, and split the loss into externalization, absorption and action closure; this card's paper borrows the absorption/closure split and removes externalization by using a deterministic tool.

neighbors.title: The Complexity Trap: Simple Observation Masking Is as Efficient as LLM Summarization for Agent Context Management
neighbors.trick: On SWE-bench Verified with SWE-agent, drop old environment observations instead of summarizing them with an LLM; cost halves and the solve rate matches or beats summarization, so the expensive context manager buys nothing measurable.

neighbors.title: ACON: Optimizing Context Compression for Long-horizon LLM Agents
neighbors.trick: Iteratively rewrite natural-language compression guidelines for observations and history from analyses of the agent's failures, then distill the compressor into a small model; peak tokens fall 26-54% on AppWorld and OfficeBench with task success held or improved; it is the compaction-recipe family this card's paper would measure, not one it measures.

theme_fit.why: tool output kept out of the context window and read back through an index is a lossy message the agent writes to its own future turns; the paper measures what it costs (where, by stage), with content held fixed by paired replay, and shows one controlled fix; this is the lane's measurement register with a mechanism and a small recipe consequence

attribution of outcome variance to who moved (agent compute vs harness delivery vs agent reading) by deterministic re-execution instead of a judge, plus benchmark validity work (42 of 200 keys defective, strict 134-item subset) and the finding that a net-zero leaderboard delta hides a ten-point evidence-use loss; triage scored 2, the full text raises it because the instrument, not the benchmark, is the contribution

same words (input tokens per item, context budget, truncation caps) but the paper reports token cost only as a side column (TOC 61.8k vs inline 65.7k vs TOC+Report 49.7k per item for GPT-5.2) and does not treat delivery as a serving or cost problem

same move, different field: re-running the exact inputs an agent produced under a deterministic reference to label each step is the per-step audit shape of L5, but the simulator is aqueous geochemistry and nothing about physics fidelity or RL exploitation is touched

limitations_as_complaints: I can show that GPT-5.1, 5.2 and 5.4 answer from their own output files and Sonnet 4.6 does not, but every model is closed and reached through an API, the Claude agents ran at temperature 0 without extended thinking and the GPT agents at default effort, so I cannot name the model property that drives the split or say whether it survives explicit reasoning (sec. 9, Models; Decoding and prompts).

My stage decomposition is anchored to one logged inline run per model, the four TOC runs share a single run on the 33 long-report items, conditions were run at different times against served models that can change, and the fixed-computation replay exists for GPT-5.2 only; the API budget left cells empty and I tested one wording of each instruction (sec. 9, Runs; Decoding and prompts; Table 8).

My 'seen' label is a numeric match at option precision, which a hand audit confirms on 52 of 58 trajectories but which counts a matching number printed for another reaction step as the keyed value; and of 24 item-level TOC losses I read, only 7 were caused by the retrieval channel while 15 were build failures that churn between runs, so the mechanism is visible only in the aggregate decomposition, not at the item level (App. C, Reliability; Manual audit).
